parsing_res_list.block_content: ## GENERAL EDITOR'S INTRODUCTION

The Garland Bibliographies of Modern Critics and Critical Schools series is intended to provide bibliographic treatment of major critics and critical schools of the twentieth century. Each volume includes an introduction that surveys the critic's life, career, influence, and achievement, or, in the case of the volumes devoted to a critical school, presents an account of its central figures, origins, relations to other critical movements and trends, and the like.

Each volume is fully annotated and contains listings for both primary and secondary materials. The annotations are meant to be ample and detailed, in order to explain clearly, especially for a reader coming to a critic or critical school for the first time, the point and purpose of a book or essay. In this sense, the bibliographies are also designed to be critical guides. We hope that the volumes will inform and stimulate the reader even as they give basic information about what material exists and where it may be located.

We have tried to include as many of the most important critics and critical schools in this series as possible, but some have been omitted. Some critics and critical schools have already received (or are in the process of receiving) adequate treatment, and we see no need to duplicate the efforts of others.

WILLIAM E. CAIN

Wellesley College

This bibliography of works by and about Arthur O. Lovejoy appears in a series devoted to modern literary critics and critical schools but will also be useful to those who know Lovejoy as a philosopher, historian of ideas, and political, social, and academic activist. The bibliography brings together Lovejoy's writings in all of these areas, as well as books, essays, and reviews by his contemporaries and later scholars dealing with his work. The bibliography is divided into three parts: Part One, works written by Lovejoy; Part Two, secondary sources dealing directly with Lovejoy's career and writing or having some direct bearing on them; and Part Three, secondary sources providing background for a fuller understanding of Lovejoy's career and work. The index lists authors, titles, and subjects.
I have attempted to provide a complete bibliography of both Lovejoy's writings and of the secondary sources. In the case of Lovejoy's works I believe this bibliography is exhaustive, with the exception of Lovejoy's letters to the editors of various newspapers. Lovejoy was an inveterate letter writer and while I have included those letters of which I am aware, I have not attempted to make a systematic search of every possible newspaper. Many of the letters included are known only because of clippings in the Lovejoy Collection at Johns Hopkins and, as a result, I have not been able to provide page numbers for the citation in every instance. The secondary sources are complete, so far as I know, to June 1981, though in a few instances I have been unable to obtain copies for annotation. Several of the essays were not indexed in any of the standard indices, and there may be others which I have not found, though I am confident that their number is very small.

parsing_res_list.block_content: ## INTRODUCTION

Arthur O. Lovejoy was not primarily a literary critic although the history of ideas pioneered by him in the 1920s and 1930s had considerable influence on literary criticism in America. Lovejoy was first and foremost a philosopher attempting to provide an intelligible account of the world in which he lived. He was no narrow specialist, however, and his intellectual interests ranged widely, from ancient religions to the literature of the Enlightenment and the Romantic periods and the pre-Darwinian evolutionary theories. He brought to the history of ideas and to literary criticism a philosophical disposition to analyze and to discriminate and a willingness to break down disciplinary boundaries in pursuit of understanding. Understanding was possible only by knowing the precise meaning of the terms employed by the writers so that any confusions and ambiguities became abundantly clear. Lovejoy's emphasis on the logical relations of ideas was a legacy of his philosophical interests and training.

Arthur Oncken Lovejoy was born in Berlin on October 10, 1873, to Wallace William Lovejoy, a Boston medical student studying in Germany, and Sara Oncken Lovejoy, his German wife. Within eighteen months the Lovejoys had moved to Boston where Wallace attempted to establish a medical practice. The adjustment proved difficult for Sara and she died of an accidental drug overdose in April 1875. The next several years were particularly difficult for young Arthur and his father who were often separated. Wallace's remarriage in 1881 to Emmeline Dunton brought new stability to the family. Wallace had, in the meantime, given up medicine for the Protestant Episcopal ministry. Arthur received his early education in the schools of Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey as Wallace was called to various ministerial posts. Following Arthur's graduation from the Germantown (Pa.) Academy in 1891, the family moved to Oakland, California, where Wallace had accepted a teaching position.

Lovejoy entered the University of California at Berkeley in 1891. His course of study emphasized the humanities and languages though he increasingly came under the influence of the philosopher George Holmes. However, though Lovejoy would eventually reject Howison's idealism, the Berkeley professor helped shift Lovejoy's prime interest from religion to philosophy and inculcated in his student habits of skepticism, rigorous inquiry, and constant pursuit after truth.

The years at Berkeley also saw Lovejoy begin to wean himself from the evangelical influence of his father. During his difficulties Wallace had found solace in accepting Christ as his savior and had given up medicine for the ministry. He had tried to induce in his adolescent son the same beliefs and religious fervor which had sustained him. The younger Lovejoy, though he respected his father's views, did not share them fully and viewed philosophy and social service as viable alternatives to evangelical religion. Lovejoy gained his father's grudging acceptance of his views following a protracted dispute which lasted long after he had left Berkeley. Father and son could agree on the value of social service, and Lovejoy began at Berkeley a long commitment to social and political activism by becoming involved with the work of a local settlement house.

Following his graduation in 1895 Lovejoy was determined to do graduate work in philosophy at Harvard. His father, however, wanted him to enter ministerial studies, though he eventually and reluctantly acceded to his son's wishes. Lovejoy attended Harvard from 1895 to 1899 during the Golden Age of Josiah Royce, William James, and George Santayana. Royce and James clearly had the most influence on the young philosopher. He studied Royce's Absolute Idealism closely and respected his professor's beliefs, but he came increasingly to believe that absolute systems were untenable. James's pluralism and pragmatism proved initially more attractive, though Lovejoy would in the succeeding decades become a major critic of pragmatism. It was at Harvard that Lovejoy began to develop his own views. Here the problem of time first came to the fore, and Lovejoy recognized that for him the problem of making a changing, developing, pluralistic universe intelligible without resorting to absolutes was central.

Harvard, and then went to Paris in 1898–1899 working at the Bibliothèque Nationale and studying at the Sorbonne, ostensibly in preparation for taking the Ph.D. The M.A. was, however, the only advanced degree Lovejoy would earn, a decision probably made on the advice of James, who had a low opinion of the Ph.D.

Lovejoy began his career as a teacher of philosophy at Stanford University in 1899. While there he became active in the controversy surrounding the dismissal of the economist and sociologist E. A. Ross. Lovejoy refused to support the actions of the university administration, publicly aired his differences, and resigned in protest in April 1901. This incident convinced Lovejoy of the necessity of guaranteeing academic freedom to university and college faculties, a conviction he carried to his grave. After his resignation he secured an appointment to Washington University in St. Louis, where he taught from 1901 until 1907. During the 1907–1908 academic year he was a visiting professor at Columbia University and, then, from 1908 to 1910 he was professor of philosophy at the University of Missouri-Columbia. In 1910 he accepted an appointment to The Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, where he remained until his retirement in 1938.

The years between his appointment at Stanford and World War I were fruitful and busy. He was laying the foundation for a distinguished career as a professor of philosophy, but he did not neglect either his commitment to activism or his scholarship. Lovejoy was deeply involved in settlement work in St. Louis and Baltimore. He also promoted the rights of college professors, particularly after he arrived at Johns Hopkins. During the first fifteen years of the century Lovejoy published widely on the history of religion and history of philosophy, on philosophy, particularly pragmatism and realism, and on social and political questions. His articles on the history of religion and philosophy were early essays in the method of the history of ideas which he would refine in the 1920s and 1930s. Much of his work in philosophy was critical, particularly of pragmatism and the new realism, though he did begin to construct his own views based on epistemological and psychophysical dualism and on temporalism. On political and social matters he ranged from the power of the president to child labor legislation and pension plans for college teachers.

The second decade of the century saw Lovejoy increasingly active in the professional and political arenas. His concern for academic freedom led him in 1913 to take the first steps toward the establishment of a national organization of professors, an effort which culminated in the formation of the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) in 1915. Lovejoy served as the first secretary of the organization and as president in 1919 (96). His views profoundly influenced the position of the AAUP regarding academic freedom (82, 95).

After war broke out in Europe in 1914 Lovejoy supported the British and French against the Germans and repeatedly urged American aid to the Allies. He believed that a German victory would extinguish freedom in Europe and threaten it everywhere. Once the United States entered the war in April 1917, Lovejoy enthusiastically supported the war effort. He wrote frequent letters to the editors of newspapers, argued that conscientious objection was untenable, participated in the propaganda efforts of the National Security League and the YMCA, visited Europe as a member of a special delegation, modified and weakened the AAUP's position on academic freedom in wartime (95), and generally tried to contribute to an Allied victory. Only occasionally, as with his 1916 presidential address to the American Philosophical Association (91), did Lovejoy contribute to the philosophical and historical debates of these years.

When the war ended, Lovejoy turned his attention to scholarship, particularly in philosophy and in the history of ideas. He continued to criticize pragmatic theories, especially those of John Dewey (102), but he also began to work out the details of his own dualistic position in essays like "The Anomaly of Knowledge" (113). The importance of evolution in Lovejoy's philosophy became more evident following the publication of "The Discontinuities of Evolution" (118) in 1924 and "The Meanings of 'Emergence' and Its Modes" (124) in 1927. Lovejoy brought his critical and analytical skills to bear on the problem of knowledge in his 1928 Carus Lectures, which were published as The Revolt Against Dualism (2) in 1930. Here Lovejoy attacked the various adherents of monism, including Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead, and defended his own versions of epistemological and psychophysical dualism. During the 1920s and 1930s Lovejoy also did much to establish the history of ideas as a legitimate method of inquiry. He did not begin by issuing methodological manifestos but rather established the discipline through his example of carefully and extensively researched scholarly essays. Most of his essays concerned thinkers and intellectual movements of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. These essays, such as "On the Discrimination of Romanticisms" (119), were marked by careful discrimination and analysis of terms and ideas, a willingness to cross traditional disciplinary boundaries, and the conviction that philosophical rigor ought to be applied to the historical study of ideas, their transmission, and diffusion. The application of these methods can best be seen in Lovejoy's 1933 William James Lectures at Harvard, published in 1936 as The Great Chain of Being (5). Here Lovejoy traced the history of three "unit-ideas," plenitude, continuity, and gradation, from their Platonic origins to the early nineteenth century. He argued that for most of the history of western civilization these three ideas, united in the form of the chain of being, had structured the way we understood the universe. The conception of the chain of being changed over its long history and Lovejoy traced the vicissitudes and permutations of the idea in the writings of Plotinus, Aquinas, Spinoza, Leibniz, Pope, Schelling, and a host of lesser figures. Ultimately, he concluded that the history of this idea demonstrated that the idea of the chain of being had been a failure, for no absolute conception of the world could ever be reconciled with the temporality of our existence.

After spending a year at Harvard in 1937–1938, he retired from Johns Hopkins in 1938 to devote himself to his research. a teacher (518), but Lovejoy was not interested in expanding his teaching or the philosophy department at Johns Hopkins. His influence derived, rather, from his writing and in the history of ideas, at least, he instructed an entire generation of literary scholars.

Lovejoy's retirement did not mean a cessation of scholarly activity. He was soon deeply involved in the planning for a new journal, The Journal of the History of Ideas, which began publication in 1940. Lovejoy also renewed his commitment to social and political activism in the face of the totalitarian threats in Europe and Asia in the 1930s. Although Lovejoy is most often cited as a historian of ideas, he considered himself to be primarily a philosopher and his work is best understood from that perspective. Philosophy was fundamental for him because it enabled him to break the shackles of evangelical religion imposed by his father and to construct an intelligible account of the universe on rational, though not absolutistic, principles. This quest for an intelligible account of the world underlay his work in both philosophy and the history of ideas.

In the 1890s when Lovejoy began to study philosophy idealism was the reigning orthodoxy and both George Holmes Howison at Berkeley and Josiah Royce at Harvard were among the leading exponents. Their student, however, quickly became disillusioned with idealism, especially with the more absolutistic idealism of Royce. Idealism seemed to contradict one irreducible fact, the temporality of our experience of the real world. No absolute could be totally absolute and still contain a developing evolving world in which the experience of time was primary. Lovejoy eventually developed what he called "temporalistic realism" (130) based on the existence of a real evolving world in which time was a central experience and which could be rationally understood.

Lovejoy rejected the idealism of Royce as too absolute and rigid, but he was equally unwilling to follow William James to the extremes of pluralism, voluntarism, and irrationality. Often considered a severe critic of pragmatism, Lovejoy was, nonetheless, sympathetic to several major pragmatic tenets. James's pluralistic universe seemed more in accord with reality as Lovejoy saw it and the older philosopher's voluntarism was consistent with development and evolution over time. Yet, Lovejoy felt that James often went too far toward irrationalism; the world was pluralistic and evolving, but there must still be some basis on which to organize our experiences. For Lovejoy, that basis was reason.

professionalizing philosophers of the first twenty years of the century hoped to find a way to establish philosophical truth on the same solid grounds as scientific truth. Lovejoy believed that by using reason rigorously and cooperating in the effort philosophers ought to be able to resolve philosophical problems definitively. He was very active in attempting to get the American Philosophical Association to support this notion and his presidential address, "On Some Conditions of Progress in Philosophical Inquiry" (91), was devoted to the problem. Though other philosophers shared his general views, no coherent, all-embracing reform of philosophy was ever accomplished.

Lovejoy turned instead to developing his own ideas concerning the problem of how we can know anything in a contingent, evolving, and, yet, real world. His epistemological positions were most fully developed in "The Anomaly of Knowledge" (113) and in The Revolt Against Dualism (2). Lovejoy was both an epistemological and psychophysical dualist; that is, all knowing is indirect and mediated by ideas and the world is made up of both material objects and minds and neither is to be viewed merely as a manifestation of the other. Lovejoy conceded that anomalies remained in his account of knowing, but he argued that the existence of ideas gave man a means of knowing the world, if only indirectly, and that only a dualistic account preserved the reality of the existing world and did justice to our modes of perceiving it.

Reason and rationality were equally central to Lovejoy's ethical beliefs, which he first expressed in "The Desires of the Self-Conscious" (33) and much later in "Terminal and Adjectival Values" (162) and Reflections on Human Nature (12). Drawing on the ideas of David Hume and Adam Smith, Lovejoy argued that reason alone was not capable of motivating ethical behavior; only desire and emotion could motivate man's actions. Our greatest desire was for a sense of self-esteem; we desired the approval or approbation of our peers and wanted to avoid their disapproval or disapprobation. Reason entered this scheme because we could rationally choose those actions that will win approbation and avoid those that brought disapprobation. Desire thus remained the spring of action, though rational choice served as a critical prelude to the experience of particular kinds of desire and, subsequently, action.

Although Lovejoy was an active participant in the philosophical debates of the early twentieth century, his philosophy has had relatively little lasting influence. In part, that derives from Lovejoy's role as a critic of idealism, pragmatism, monism, and absolutism. He never fully worked out the implications of his own positions, preferring, instead, to criticize the errant views of his colleagues. Nor did he have any students who developed and defended his views. In addition, the critic, though he performs a vital function, is often relegated to a secondary role in comparison with the originators of new departures in philosophy, such as Charles Sanders Pierce or William James. Finally, since the 1930s philosophical thinking has developed along lines different from those Lovejoy pursued. The old debates about idealism versus realism or monism versus dualism lost their cogency under the impact of logical positivism and subsequent developments in analytical philosophy and logical thought. When Lovejoy is cited by philosophers today it is most often as a historian of philosophy and of ideas, not as an original thinker in philosophy.

It is as a historian of ideas that Lovejoy has had the greatest influence on literary criticism. His work in the 1920s and 1930s brought a new vigor and rigor to studies of the seventeenth, eighteenth, and early nineteenth centuries. Lovejoy emphasized the primacy of studying ideas and the necessity for careful, though wide-ranging, scholarship. He shattered the traditional boundaries of literary scholarship by demonstrating that Milton, or Pope, or the Romantics could not be fully understood unless one understood the philosophical, scientific, religious, cultural, and personal implications of the ideas employed by these men. Such an understanding was beyond the capacity of any one individual and Lovejoy was a powerful advocate for cooperation in literary studies. In spite of the importance of his literary studies, they were, in the main, an offshoot of his philosophical concerns.

It was Lovejoy's essays of the 1920s and 1930s that had the greatest impact on literary criticism and that established the history of ideas as a separate discipline. He now concentrated on the thought of the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries, attempting to clarify the confusion and ambiguities in the thinking of that period and in the contemporary literary criticism. Perhaps his single most influential article was "On the Discrimination of Romanticisms" (119), in which he argued that there was no single Romanticism in the early nineteenth century, but, rather, many romanticisms in the history of thought and culture. He urged his colleagues to define precisely which romanticism they were discussing in order to avoid the confusion which had plagued the field.

The 1930s saw the publication of two larger studies: Primitivism and Related Ideas in Antiquity (4), written and edited with George Boas, and The Great Chain of Being (5). Primitivism was supposed to be the first volume in a documentary history of the idea of primitivism, but it was the only volume ever published. The book was a cooperative effort with Lovejoy and Boas, as well as several other colleagues, attempting to provide all the documents related to the idea of primitivism in the ancient world. They provided the original document, translations, and commentary. The magnitude of the task and the problems of cooperation were more difficult than anticipated and the subsequent volumes were never completed.

ideas were constructed. The construction of an idea like the chain of being in all its manifestations was marked by ambiguity, logical weaknesses, and other problems. It is these ambiguities and logical fallacies that Lovejoy traced and attempted to clarify, particularly in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century thought when the idea of the chain reached its highest development.

Lovejoy's study of the history of the chain of being was not simply an exercise in methodology. He chose to study an idea with particular relevance to important philosophical questions. The chain of being was an absolute, static conception of the universe in which the fullness of creation in all its gradations from top to bottom must exist at the same time. What Lovejoy discovered was that various seventeenth- and eighteenth-century thinkers, prodded in part by new developments in science, had begun to expose the weaknesses in the idea of the chain. Lovejoy's careful discrimination of the meaning of ideas and meticulous tracing of their diffusion and influence was a significant break from the more personal and moralistic approach that had dominated criticism. Lovejoy's approach was not without its personal bias and moral implications, but he emphasized the importance of establishing the meaning of ideas in their literary and cultural contexts and the necessity to be sensitive to the diverse and often ambiguous use of ideas. Lovejoy's method enabled literary critics, especially academic critics, to introduce greater rigor and precision into their studies. Academic criticism thus could become less a matter of personal reflection and more clearly professional and scientific scholarship.

In the last fifteen years Lovejoy's methods in the history of ideas have come under increasing scrutiny and criticism. The prime focus of critics like Thomas Bredsdorff (331), Jaakko Hintikka (359), Nils Bjorn Kvastad (369), and Maurice Mandelbaum (378), has been Lovejoy's conception of the "unit-idea." Lovejoy conceived unit-ideas as the building blocks from which more complex ideas were constructed. The historian of ideas traced the ways in which thinkers used those unit-ideas to construct more complex ideas. Writers were not always sensitive to the logical relations between ideas nor to the ambiguities which crept into their thinking and part of the task of the historian of ideas was to clarify the confusions that had appeared in the meaning and use of ideas. The criticism has been along two lines: that there are certain logical, philosophical, or practical problems with Lovejoy's conception of a unit-idea, or that if his conception is indeed tenable, then plenitude, gradation, and continuity do not fit the criteria of a unit-idea. The first mode of criticism, if sustained, is the more telling, but the critics do not seem to have totally rejected the general notion of a unit-idea though they have problems with Lovejoy's particular formulation. In any case, Lovejoy has had his supporters, such as Moltke S. Gram and

Richard M. Martin (355), who have defended his conception of a unit-idea.

Both as a philosopher and as a historian of ideas, Arthur O. Lovejoy was most influential in the first forty years of this century. His acute, critical mind forced idealists, pragmatists, and monists to sharpen their arguments even if they were not always convinced of Lovejoy's positions. His efforts to establish a more scientific philosophy and temporalistic critical realism helped shape philosophic debate until the early thirties. Lovejoy's essays in the history of ideas and The Great Chain of Being opened new avenues of study for intellectual historians and literary critics in the 1920s and after. Finally, his activism on behalf of academic freedom helped ensure that scholars would be relatively free to pursue their studies without external pressures. Lovejoy was not without his contemporary critics, and scholars since his death have subjected his work, particularly in the history of ideas, to increasing scrutiny. Whatever the ultimate fate of his particular positions, Lovejoy will remain a model of rigorous inquiry and scholarly integrity.

chain of being as an organizing scheme for the universe from its Platonic origins to its decline in importance in the early nineteenth century. The general conception of the chain had its origin in the coming together, most clearly in Neo-Platonic thought, of three unit-ideas: plenitude, the idea that the universe is completely filled by a diversity of creatures; continuity, the idea that there was some linear series of classes linking all forms of existence in a continuum; and gradation, the idea that all things can be graded within the continuum. Before he traces the history of these ideas in detail Lovejoy discusses the methodological bases for his study of ideas. He argues that unit-ideas are the "component elements" of more complex intellectual structures and, hence, the proper focus of attention. These more complex structures, however, are also the product of "motives and reasons," which may contribute to "the production of very diverse conclusions."

Lovejoy applied these methods to his history of the chain of being. The three constituent ideas were first articulated in western thought by Plato and Aristotle, though it was the Neo-Platonist Plotinus who first brought them together in the fruitful combination that would so influence our idea of the universe. Lovejoy then traced the vicissitudes and permutations of these ideas through medieval thought, especially that of Aquinas, and early modern science and philosophy, particularly in Spinoza and Leibniz, to their flowering in eighteenth-century philosophy, literature, and science. He discovered that as the idea of the chain was elaborated and the implications explored, the idea of the chain as an organizing principle was weakened. Scientific studies in search of the missing links eventually led to a conclusion that the notion of becoming was more tenable than that of the chain of being. This "temporalizing of the chain of being" in the eighteenth century led to its downfall by the early nineteenth century. Friedrich Schelling was the first, according to Lovejoy, to reject the chain of being in favor of becoming. The moral which Lovejoy derived from this history was that absolute, static conceptions of the universe are doomed to failure. The Great Chain of Being, then, is important not only as the history of a central idea in western thought and as the prime example of the history of ideas, but also as a testament to Lovejoy's efforts to establish the idea of

Argues that a university should be judged from two points of view: as "primarily an instrument for intellectual discipline and the promotion of scholarship" and as "a member in a complicated social organism." Examines the social role of the University of Paris, which he finds lacking in comparison with its intellectual achievements. 48. "The Argument for Organic Evolution Before 'The Origin of Species.'"  $ \underline{\text{Popular Science Monthly}} $, 75 (1909), 499-514, 537-49.

Surveys recent developments in the histories of the notion of the Will to Live and "the doctrine of cosmic and organic evolution." 52. "Pragmatism and Realism."  $ \underline{JP} $, 6 (1909), 575-80.

Examines W.P. Montague's series of essays entitled "May a Realist Be a Pragmatist?" (386) and takes issue with Montague on several points. Argues that pragmatism is "a modern expression of the motive which in certain other expressions is known as nominalism or positivism." Also asserts that pragmatism's "distinctiveness consists precisely in the fact that it combines instrumentalism and the method of nominalism." Against Montague, Lovejoy thinks these two motives are "harmonious." Lovejoy concludes that Montague has not proven that a pragmatist must be a realist. On the contrary, he argues that a pragmatist "ought to be either an idealist or what for the present I can only call an anti-dualistic x."
Reprinted in 13.
53. "Some Aspects of Darwin's Influence upon Modern Thought."  $ \underline{\text{Bulletin of the Washington University Association}} $, 7 (1909), 85-99.

Considers "the influence of the hypothesis of natural selection upon the philosophical and religious reflection of the last fifty years." Argues that it was the idea of the transformation of species that was Darwin's most notable contribution. Darwin's ideas on natural selection were important in "the movement of modern thought away from teleological explanations of natural processes and towards a statement of the law of occurrence of all such processes in consistently mechanistic terms." Darwin's ideas have had a mixed impact on man's view of the world he inhabits: "As the most effective of the promoters of evolutionist views in biology, he has been also a promoter of cheerfulness and optimism; but as the author of the hypothesis of natural selection he has seemed to give a sort of scientific version of the melancholy picture of the nature of things." Finally, Lovejoy argues that while some moralists have drawn heavily on Darwin's ideas, he believes that natural selection can play only a negative role of checking the "all too widely aberrant variations" in ethical theory derived from beliefs in the nature of man.

54. "Kant and Evolution."  $ \underline{\text{Popular Science Monthly}} $, 77 (1910) 538-53, 78 (1911), 36-51.

Argues that in spite of assertions that Kant was a pioneer of evolutionism, he at most flirted with accepting the theory of biological evolution and on several occasions clearly rejected the theory. This misconception concerning Kant's views on evolution was the result of "taking certain of his expressions apart from their contexts and in disregard of the meanings which he was accustomed to give certain terms." Examines several of Kant's works which pertain to the subject. Concludes that Kant "never once professed belief in the transformist hypothesis; nor did he ever show an ability to apprehend clearly either the precise meaning or the force of the considerations which could even then be adduced in favor of that doctrine."

55. "The Place of the Time Problem in Contemporary Philosophy."  $ \underline{JP} $, 7 (1910), 683-93.

Attempts to outline the major philosophical positions in the contemporary dispute between, on the one side, rationalism, eternalism, idealism, and this-worldliness, and, on the other side, anti-intellectualism, pragmatic nominalism or radical empiricism, realism, and temporalism. Offers five observations on the dispute: 1) that the four newer tendencies are not equally opposed to the older views; 2) that adherents of the new views are not agreed on possible combinations of the different positions; 3) that temporalism of some variety seems present in most combinations of the new views; 4) that the eternalism of the older philosophy is most consistently opposed; and 5) that the eternalism and this-worldliness of the "idealistic systems are essentially incongruous." Attacks eternalistic philosophies and concludes by defending "the reality of temporal transition."

"The Treatment of 'Opposition' in Formal Logic."  $ \underline{JP} $, 7 (1910), 101-105.

Argues that the method of teaching the subject of the opposition of propositions has been essentially unchanged since Aristotle. 57. "Buffon and the Problem of Species."  $ \underline{\text{Popular Science Monthly}} $，79 (1911)，464-73，544-67.

Describes the six different interpretations of Buffon's view of transformism, all of which seem to be "either inadequate or erroneous, though all may be said in some measure to be founded on fact." Through a close analysis of Buffon's language and the chronology of his utterances on the subject, Lovejoy attempts to clarify Buffon's ideas on transformism. Argues that his "work both fostered and hindered the propagation of evolutionary ideas in biology." Buffon was one of the first thinkers to "put the hypothesis of organic evolution before his contemporaries in clear and definite form" and to accustom men to think on a greatly enlarged time-frame. He also, however, "did more than any other eighteenth-century writer to check the progress of evolutionism, especially with regard to the definition of species." Lovejoy concludes that Buffon "must be regarded as having done more than any man of his time to counteract the tendency which he also, perhaps, did more than any other to promote."

condemn the "competitive industrial system ... simply because it is competitive." Economic competition is contrary to the "Christian law of love." In examining the position of the Christian socialist Lovejoy focuses on the ways in which the present economic system is competitive. The collective bargaining process can be seen as an instance of buyer-seller competition and, thus, is contrary to Christian ethics. Examines critically various arguments designed to support the idea of economic competition. Suggests that "Christianity's yearning" for harmony between classes and interests "would find full realisation in a concrete economic order only through a scheme of complete equality in distribution." Opens with some general comments on new directions in philosophy and notes that while he welcomes the diversity, he can not share the enthusiasm of many adherents of the new ideas. 79. "On the Existence of Ideas."  $ \underline{\text{The Johns Hopkins University Circular}} $, 33 (1914), 178-235.

Defends the existence of "sensations, of images, of ideas, of mental states, of 'subjective appearances,' and the possibility of 'introspection'" against recent philosophers who have denied the existence of one or more of these entities. Concedes that "consciousness does not exist as an observable item amongst the objects of perception," but argues that it does not follow from that fact that consciousness does not exist at all. Believes that what philosophers are trying to deny is not the existence of consciousness, which can not know physical things directly, but the existence of ideas, which consciousness might know. Traces recent arguments against the existence of ideas and examines the philosophical implications if it can be proven that ideas do or do not exist. Argues that "the belief in mental representations is not ... a groundless and functionless philosophical superstition, but a natural product of human reflection upon certain common human experiences." 86. "On the Meaning of 'Romantic' in Early German Romanti-cism."  $ \underline{\text{MLN}} $, 31 (1916), 385-96, 32 (1917), 65-77.

Discusses several interpretations of the origin and meaning of "romantic" in late eighteenth-century Germany and concludes that previous studies have been inaccurate. Argues that Friedrich Schlegel had applied the term throughout the 1790s to several types of literature as "an ordinary historical epithet." By 1798 the word contained "aesthetic and philosophical connotations." Concludes that "the theory of Romanticism was ... a by-product of the prevalent classicism of the early seventeen-nineties." Theorists like Schegel tried to clarify more completely the classical principles and the opposed principles of modernism. Schlegel, and others, eventually embraced what they had initially condemned, becoming converts to the "Romantic doctrine of art." The term "romantic" was chosen because it had "a less fixedly chronological import than modern, and was therefore more capable of connoting certain aesthetic characteristics, the exclusively modern origin of which was significant but not the essential fact."

95. (With Edward Capps and A.A. Young). "Report of the Committee on Academic Freedom in Wartime."  $ \underline{\text{BAAUP}} $, 4 (February-March 1918), 29-47.

Attempts to formulate for the American Association of University Professors "an interpretation of academic freedom with especial reference to the extraordinary situation created by the war." Notes that there can be no question about the loyalty of most members of the teaching profession. There are two demands placed on citizens in a time of war: to make the sacrifices demanded and to ensure that "no avoidable injury is done to the permanent interests of society." Concedes that in a time of crisis the government may impose "some restrictions of normal liberty," but "such restrictions are not to be multiplied, as they tend to be, beyond real necessity." In general, the committee feels that academics should not be placed under any greater restrictions than ordinary citizens. Nonetheless, the committee argues that there are four grounds upon which a college administration may legitimately dismiss a teacher "because of his attitude or conduct in relation to the war": 1) those convicted of violating any war-related law; 2) those who encourage others "to resist or evade" the draft or other military regulations; 3) those who "seek to disuade others from rendering voluntary assistance to the efforts of the government"; and 4) those of German or Austro-Hungarian heritage who actively support their homelands. Argues that even in these cases the usual procedural safeguards should be followed. Concludes with an appeal to all academics to aid their nation in this time of emergency. The report was largely the work of Lovejoy.

100. "Better Organization of Teachers Without Unionization." Educational Review, 60 (November 1920), 329-35.

Continues discussion of the possible unionization of teachers begun in "Teachers and Trade-Unions" (104). 101. "Pragmatism as Interactionism."  $ \underline{JP} $, 17 (1920), 589-96, 622-32.

Examines pragmatic views on the question of interactionism, especially as expressed by Boyd H. Bode in his essay in  $ \underline{\text{Creative Intelligence}} $ (522). Sees instrumentalism as a "revolt against that strange nineteenth-century aberration, epiphenomenalism." This requires, in Lovejoy's view, that instrumentalists enter into an alliance with "an honestly dualistic conception of the psychophysical relation." Proposes to address the question of the "logical relations" of pragmatism to realism, idealism, monism, dualism, consciousness, mental states, and psychological entities. 113. "The Anomaly of Knowledge."  $ \underline{\text{University of California Publications in Philosophy}} $, 4 (1923), 3-43.

Contends that philosophers are especially suited to make scientific inquiries into the problem of having knowledge about things. Proposes to give an account of knowing and to offer an explanation of how it is possible to know anything. Concentrates on the problem of knowing things not immediately and directly present at the moment of experience. Knowledge, then, is "a kind of evocation of the absent." Defends the notion of representative ideas and of representative or mediate knowledge. Describes the lesser and greater anomalies of knowledge. The lesser raises the question of how a physical being can have knowledge of things, such as ideas, which are not physical. The greater anomaly poses the problem of knowing by having "within the field of our experience at a given moment objects which we must at the same time conceive as existing entirely outside of that field." Argues that the only way to solve the greater anomaly is to accept the lesser; that is, all knowing occurs through the mediation of representative ideas.

118. "The Discontinuities of Evolution."  $ \underline{\text{University of California Publications in Philosophy}} $, 5 (1924), 173-220.

Begins by discussing the ideas of George Holmes. Howson on evolution and criticizing the eternalism of his philosophy. Notes that many contemporary philosophers have come to accept the notion that the "evolutional process" exhibits breaks or chasms giving rise to "absolute novelties" or "discontinuous variations." Traces the development of these ideas in late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century thinkers, including Bergson, Whitehead, Baldwin, and Sellars. Focuses the bulk of the paper on problems concerning "the evolution of natural laws." A discontinuity in the evolution of laws would manifest itself as "the appearance of some correlation of events or method of action which cannot be described by the generalizations that would have correctly described all the correlations of previous events or methods of action." Distinguishes his theory from the tychism of C.S. Peirce and then defines the ways in which laws may be said to be discontinuous. Examines the implications of the existence of discontinuities with regard to laws applying to the inorganic and organic realms and especially on the possibility of reducing all laws to one. Focuses the final part of the essay on the question of whether mental and physical entities can be described by the same law or whether the laws describing mental and physical activity are discontinuous. Suggests that intelligent foresight represents an example of a discontinuity in the evolution of natural laws.

129. "The Dialectical Argument Against Absolute Simultaneity."  $ \underline{JP} $, 27 (1930), 617-32, 645-54.

Argues that if Einstein is right in extending the notion of relativity from space to time, his theories will force a radical and wide-ranging reconsideration of logic, evolution, and "the significance of the time-process." In such a situation, philosophers have a duty to examine the philosophical implications of Einstein's theories. Einstein's argument concerning "the unreality of absolute simultaneity" is really philosophical and thus subject to philosophical scrutiny. Since we have only "one unequivocal notion of simultaneity which is given us through experience," we ought not to confuse this fact by employing the same notion to explain certain experimental results. In the second part of the essay Lovejoy examines Einstein's conception of "simultaneity-at-a-distance" and concludes that it is both arbitrary and circular. Other explanations, which do less violence to the ordinary concept of simultaneity, can explain the experimental evidence as fully as Einstein's theories.

Examines the paradoxes of the Special Theory of Relativity, particularly the paradox of the time-retarding journey. 137. "The Chinese Origin of a Romanticism."  $ \underline{\text{The Journal of English and German Philology}} $, 32 (1933), 1-20.

Asserts that the vogue for Chinese gardens in eighteenth-century England was part of an "incipient Romanticism" which initiated "the gospel of irregularity" in the canons of aesthetic taste. The Chinese model of gardening began to exercise an influence before Pope and Addison and drew upon widespread respect in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries for Chinese achievements. Traces the advocates of the Chinese style of gardening from Sir William Temple through Pope and Addison to Sir William Chambers. Argues that while Temple and Chambers shared an enthusiasm for Chinese gardens, Temple emphasized art imitating nature, whereas Chambers saw gardening as a "conscious and deliberate art, transcending the limitations and 'vulgarity' of nature." Chambers's work, ironically, contributed to the decline of the Chinese garden as an arbiter of taste. This episode is crucial in the history of modern taste, for it marks the occasion when "the ideals of regularity, simplicity, uniformity, and easy logical intelligibility were first openly impugned." See 134.
Reprinted in a revised and enlarged version in 10.
138. "Dualism and the Paradox of Reference."  $ \underline{JP} $, 30 (1933), 589-606.

Responds to C.A. Strong's "The Missing Link in Epistemology" (421) by examining both the areas of agreement and disagreement. Part of the problem lies in a misunderstanding of what exactly is present to the consciousness when referring occurs. Lovejoy attempts to make clear the nature of transcendent reference as he conceives it. Deals also with the problems of memory and perception as raised by Strong and tries to clarify his own position. On the issue of perception, Lovejoy contends that the difficulties rise because of Strong's misapprehension of the spatial distinction between datum and object. Concludes by arguing that Strong's "sensori-motor theory is irrelevant to the question of the  $ \underline{\text{modus operandi}} $ of referential experience."

Responds to C.A. Strong's "The Missing Link in Epistemology" (421) by examining both the areas of agreement and disagreement. 151. "Culbertson's International Armed Force."  $ \underline{\text{Free World}} $, 6 (1943), 463-69.

Argues that any effective international peace-keeping organization must have at its disposal "some effective type of armed force." Concedes, however, that there is considerable dispute over almost every proposal concerning such a force. Proposes to give the proposal of Ely Culbertson a "dispassionate analytical examination." Will judge Culbertson's proposal on the criteria of the probability of its adoption, its probable effectiveness, and the likelihood of its causing greater evils. Argues that Culbertson's plan, as a whole, has certain weaknesses, but that "certain features of his system ought to find a place in any plan for collective security that does not presuppose the general relinquishment by national states of effective armaments of their own."

One can find in Herder's writings "two normative principles that were destined to find a place in the German 'Romantic' ideology": first, that towards "all the elements of all cultures other than one's own ... one should cultivate a catholicity of appreciation and understanding, based upon the historical necessitarianism and historical optimism" and, second, "a kind of particularism," a belief that everyone had been placed in a particular historical and cultural situation. Discusses the implication of these somewhat contradictory ideas for Herder and his differences from other thinkers of the period.

159. "'Nature' and Norm in Tertullian." Essays in the History of Ideas. Baltimore: The Johns Hopkins University Press, 1948, pp. 308-338.

Argues that Tertullian carried over from "pagan sources into his teaching as Christian apologist and theologian a settled presumption that in 'nature,' in some sense or senses of the term, are to be found valid norms of belief and conduct." Illustrates Tertullian's use of "nature" through extensive quotation. Concludes that Tertullian "presents a chapter of considerable interest and importance in the long and curious history of the practice of deriving epistemological and ethical norms from the conceptions which ... had come to be associated with the word 'nature.' The two most important implications of Tertullian's use of "nature" lay in his assumption that nature gives to man a uniform reason by which simple and fundamental truths may be known and in his belief "that the primary and generic propensities and appetites of man, being due to 'nature,' or 'the God of nature,' are good, and therefore ought not to be denied their normal gratification." theorist must show that his "prescriptions are relevant to ... the phenomenon of voluntary choice," that he must be aware of the ways in which men's choices are determined and influenced, and must recognize that choice can be determined only by "some emotive state or desire." Draws on the writings of David Hume to support his argument that reason alone can not determine choice unless accompanied by some desire. 268. "The New Submarine Crisis."  $ \underline{\text{New York Times}} $, March 30, 1916, 12.

Argues that the time has past when a German apology for the sinking of ships with the loss of American lives is sufficient. Believes that the sinking of the  $ \underline{\text{Sussex}} $ demonstrates convincingly that the Germans have no intention of keeping their diplomatic pledges. Suggests breaking diplomatic relations with Germany if an adequate explanation of the sinking of the  $ \underline{\text{Sussex}} $ is not forthcoming.
269. "America Impartial."  $ \underline{\text{New Republic}} $, 10 (1917), 75.

Argues that if the United States is on the brink of war with Germany there are good reasons why the Wilson government might take such a step. Though both Great Britain and Germany have violated the neutral rights of the United States, Germany's infringements have been greater and have cost American lives. Also argues that "any serious weakening of the British Empire would be an incalculable and irreparable loss to the material and highest moral interests of the United States, and to the cause of free governments throughout the world." See 262, 270.
270. "Benevolent Neutrality?"  $ \underline{\text{New Republic}} $, 10 (1917), 229-30.

Addresses the question of the extent to which the United States acquiesced in the British blockade of Germany while resisting the German submarine blockade of England. Argues that the Wilson government vigorously protested the actions of both belligerents, but that a crucial difference lies in the loss of American lives as a result of German actions. The American government has not departed from neutrality to favor the allies, but it has "drawn the line at the unlawful taking of American lives and at wholesale piracy on the high seas." The editors follow Lovejoy's letter with a reply (pp. 230-32) defending their view that the Wilson government has tended to favor the Allies, but that such actions are necessary if German aggression is not to be rewarded.

271. "Government by Mendacity."  $ \underline{\text{New York Times}} $，September 17，1917，12.

Argues that none of the German government officials can be trusted to mean what they say. Part of the German preparation for war was to lie to the German people and to other nations about the true intentions of the government. The German efforts to prove that they went to war for defensive reasons were bold-faced lies and the government has not changed its method of operation. Concludes that "under the Prussian regime the German people, especially at the great crises of their national destiny, are subject to a highly organized system of Government by mendacity."
272. "To Conscientious Objectors."  $ \underline{\text{New Republic}} $, 11 (1917), 187-89.

Replying to a statement by Norman Thomas and other conscientious objectors (426) Lovejoy argues that conscientious objection as an ideal is difficult, if not impossible, to attain in the real world. He notes that the position is possible only because some men were willing to fight to achieve certain freedoms. Conscientious objectors are ethical optimists, for they disregard the "painful fact" that good must often be purchased at the cost of some evil. Morality and goodness are not the exclusive preserve of those who refuse to fight. On the question of toleration, Lovejoy concedes that because the number of conscientious objectors is small, the nation may well be "generously considerate." He makes it very clear, however, that he regards toleration of conscientious objectors as "the toleration, not simply of an erroneous opinion, but also of an anti-social attitude and mode of conduct."

290. "Proprietary Professorships and Academic Freedom."  $ \underline{\text{The Weekly Review}} $, 3 (1920), 417-18.

Summarizes briefly the relations between "chronological primitivism" and other different assumptions regarding human history. 1. (With Charles E. Trinkhaus, Jr., Ernest Nagel, and V.J. McGill). "Four Letters on Ernest Nagel's Review of Lovejoy's 'The Great Chain of Being.'"  $ \underline{\text{Science and Society}} $, 1 (1937), 410-16.

Discusses several questions raised by Charles Trinkhaus regarding Nagel's review (463) of  $ \underline{\text{The Great Chain of Being}} $ (5). Most importantly, Trinkhaus suggests that the idea of the chain reflected the hierarchy found in class structures and that Lovejoy "failed to realize the social importance of the Great Chain of Being in past history." Lovejoy responds that since he is not a "mind reader" and since most writers, on the evidence, drew their inspiration from the natural world not classes in society, he remains an "agnostic" on, for example, the relation of class structure in Athens to Plato's ideas. Doubts that economic and social causal determinants had much to do with the conception of the chain of being. Nagel also comments briefly on Trinkhaus's letter and McGill on the letters of Nagel and Lovejoy.

identified the ideas of St. Thomas with those of Plato and Plotinus regarding the contradiction between a self-sufficient good and a world in which all possibles are realized. Wilson, Daniel J.  $ \underline{\text{Arthur O. Lovejoy and the Quest for Intelligibility}} $. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1980. 248 pp.

Traces, for the first time in a full-length study, Lovejoy's life and his career as a philosopher, historian, and activist. This intellectual biography focuses on his intellectual development by examining the roots of his devotion to reason in his reaction to the uncertainties of emotion and evangelical religion, and his philosophical training. It also traces the expression of his religious beliefs, his historical methods, his philosophical positions, and his career as an activist. Lovejoy's long and distinguished career was a quest for intelligibility in a rapidly changing America. Confronted by a real world of diversity and change, Lovejoy believed that only the principles of reason could order that world, without destroying its reality, and so make our experienced universe intelligible. His career as a philosopher, historian, and activist was, in large part, an attempt to work out the implications of this conception of the universe. The first study to be based on extensive use of the manuscript sources, this biography reveals Lovejoy to be far more complex than the traditional picture of "reason-in-action" (504). While the emphasis is on Lovejoy's intellectual development, it also attempts to assess his place in the history of philosophy in the twentieth century, his role as an originator of the history of ideas, and the impact of his campaign for academic freedom.

358. Hintikka, Jaakko. "A.O. Lovejoy on Plenitude in Aristotle." Ajatus, 29 (1967), 5-11.

Argues that Lovejoy's discussion of the role of the principle of plenitude in "the history of philosophy is by no means definitive." Discusses Lovejoy's contention that the principle of plenitude can not be attributed to Aristotle. Believes he has shown that rather than rejecting the principle of plenitude, Aristotle relied on it. 359. ___. "Gaps in the Great Chain of Being: An Exercise in the Methodology of the History of Ideas."  $ \underline{\text{Proceedings and Addresses of the American Philosophical Association}} $, 49 (1976), 22-38.

Argues that Lovejoy's account of the history of plenitude in The Great Chain of Being (5) "is seriously defective, not just in its details, but also in some of its main outlines." The major flaw in the book is its methodology, particularly its reliance on the notion of "unit-ideas." Though the idea of plenitude is "perhaps as close to a unit idea as we can hope to get in history, in the last analysis it is not a unit idea." Among the problems that weaken The Great Chain of Being are Lovejoy's failure to recognize the manifold meanings of plenitude, a failure to comprehend fully how differently from his predecessors Leibniz viewed the principle, and a failure to consider the fact that the implications of the principle "are not independent of its conceptual and theoretical environment." Argues that what changed in the late Middle Ages and in the Renaissance was not only people's view of the actual world, but also their view of the possibilities, something Lovejoy failed to see. What led Lovejoy astray was "a one-sided view of the conceptual neighborhood of the principle of plenitude." Discusses ways in which the principle has influenced philosophers from Kant to G.E. Moore. The value of the history of ideas lies not in tracing unit-ideas, which Hintikka argues do not exist, but in "the teasing out of hidden ambiguities and in the discovery and clarification of the frequently surprising interrelations of different ideas." See 331, 355, 369, 378.

373. ___. "A Resurgence of 'Vicious Intellectualism.'"  $ \underline{\text{JP}} $, 48 (1951), 435-47.

Defines vicious intellectualism as "the treating of a name as an assurance that the fact named has to perfection all the characteristics which the name's definition includes and connotes." Applies this to several recent discussions of communism and the presence of communists on university faculties, including Lovejoy's "Communism versus Academic Freedom" (161). Argues that the case against communists is based on the belief that a particular communist professor is a perfect communist, in that he holds all the beliefs supposed to be held by a communist and is prepared to act on them. Lovejoy and the others who would exclude communists are too quick to assume that because a man holds a party card he is, in every respect, the perfect, ideal communist. Argues that each case should be treated separately because "we live in a world of individual persons, not of instances of abstract essences" and because "every form of vicious intellectualism in thinking about persons is a philosophical error."

Addresses the question of "the proper partition between the datum of knowledge and the object to be known." Takes up methodological problems in the history of ideas, particularly those connected with Lovejoy's notion of a "unit-idea." One problem was that Lovejoy's method failed "to yield an interpretation of the basic aim and motivating power of the system." Second, Mandelaum challenges Lovejoy's assumption that unit-ideas are "continuing ideas." While some of them may be, others may be "recurrent ideas." Notes that Lovejoy's primary concern was "to bring into sharp focus the detailed intellectual content of literary and philosophic works, and to examine their meanings and implications in a spirit of critical detachment." Lovejoy's conception, however, leaves many areas of inquiry for intellectual and cultural history untouched. 383. Michener, Richard L. "The Great Chain of Being: Three Approaches."  $ \underline{\text{Ball State University Forum}} $, 11 (1970), 60-71.

Argues that the evidence Lovejoy presents in  $ \underline{\text{The Great Chain of Being}} $ (5) "seems inadequate to support his sweeping claim that the history of the notion is found largely in its progressive diffusion" until its widespread acceptance in the eighteenth century. Examines the work of Pico Della Mirandola, John Donne, and Alexander Pope to support his contention that the idea of the chain of being played a very different role in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries from that outlined by Lovejoy. Believes that misconceptions are inevitable unless the study of an idea is closely related to the contexts in which it appears.
384. Mink, Louis O. "Change and Causality in the History of Ideas."  $ \underline{\text{Eighteenth Century Studies}} $, 2 (1968), 7-25.

Critiques Lovejoy's methodology based on three linked theses: that the history of ideas methodology has often treated ideas as things, that a "methodology of intellectual history is, and must be ... self-referential," and that the history of ideas does not need "the concept of causation." Argues that the fault in Lovejoy's methodology was that his doctrine of unit-ideas was incompatible with his doctrine of forces, of how change occurs. The "analytic method which must take unit-ideas as its objects cannot ... make conceptual sense out of the change of ideas." Lovejoy's problem was that he relied on a conception of unit-ideas that developed as a mode of thought in the natural sciences, while his doctrine of forces developed out of the rise of historical consciousness in the nineteenth century. The historian of ideas has, in fact, no need to be concerned with the problems of causal explanation. Understanding how thinker Y interpreted document X is more important than discovering that document X influenced thinker Y. Thus, declares that the "history of ideas is not a chronology of things, but the story of the development of consciousness."

409. Ritter, William E. "The Controversy Between Materialism and Vitalism: Can It Be Ended?"  $ \underline{\text{Science}} $, n.s. 33 (1911), 435-41.

Attempts to give clear meaning to the terms "materialism," "mechanism," and "vitalism" as a prelude to answering the question in the title. Reviews, briefly, the ways in which these conceptions have been treated by philosophers and concludes that materialism has received much more attention than vitalism. Suggests that materialism is "a lineal descendant in rational process of the basis of magic," while "vitalism is similarly descended from ... animism." Argues that our ideas about science and the nature of life have evolved in much the same way life itself evolved. Mechanism and vitalism are thus the modern analogues, and lineal descendants, of magic and animism. Suggests that neither can ever be reduced to the other.

See 60, 62, 183, 257, 365, 514.
410. Roberts William H. "Experience--Noun or Verb?"  $ \underline{JP} $, 38 (1941), 542-49.

Proposes that the difficulties inherent in a dualistic or monistic epistemology can be avoided by considering all experience "not as a  $ \underline{\text{thing}} $ to be denoted properly by a noun but as an activity or process that ... must be denoted by a verb." Finds that Lovejoy's discussion of knowledge in  $ \underline{\text{The Revolt Against Dualism}} $ (2) relies on three entities: 1) the stimulus, 2) the act of seeing, and 3) the object perceived. Argues that the third entity, the object seen, is unnecessary if we conceive of knowing as a process.
411. Royce, Josiah. "On Definitions and Debates."  $ \underline{JP} $, 9 (1912), 85-100.

Questions whether the recent efforts, led by Lovejoy, to structure debate and discussion in the American Philosophical Association are worth the effort. Suggests that the Committee on Definitions has structured the debate so as to exclude a significant number of philosophers from the possibility of participation. Examines in some detail the proposal of the committee and the ways it works to exclude philosophers. Supports the idea of cooperation, but argues that it must be in a framework that allows all philosophers to participate.
See 436.

412. Schmidt, Karl. "Agreement." JP, 9 (1912), 715-17.

Argues that there must be "a certain modicum of agreement" if philosophers are to accomplish anything. There must be "certain common problems," solutions to the same problem "equivalent with respect to truth," a "common set of criteria" of truth, and "agreement on the structure of the solution."
413. Skinner, Quentin. "Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas."  $ \underline{\text{History and Theory}} $，8 (1969)，3-53.

Examines what he regards as "appropriate procedures" for a historian of ideas to adopt in attempting to understand a particular work or thinker. Discusses critically the two prevailing methodologies in the history of ideas: that the context of the work determines its ultimate meaning or that the text itself is "the sole necessary key to its own meaning." The problems and difficulties inherent in a variety of expressions of these general methodologies, including Lovejoy's search for "unit-ideas," is traced in considerable detail. Concludes that it is "a mistake even to try to write intellectual biographies concentrating on the works of a given writer or to write histories of ideas tracing the morphology of a given concept over time." Argues that intellectual history is still possible if we confront, "in studying any given text, ... what its author, in writing at the time he did write for the audience he intended to address, could in practice have been intending to communicate by the utterance of this given utterance." Also believes that there is "the possibility of a dialogue between philosophical discussion and historical evidence." Skinner thus provides a good survey of the status of the history of ideas at the end of the 1960s and suggests directions the field would take in the next decade.

### 419. Stromberg, Roland N. "Lovejoy's 'Parallel' Reconsidered."  $ \underline{\text{Eighteenth Century Studies}} $, 1 (1968), 381-95.

Examines Lovejoy's generalizations on deism and classicism as set forth in "The Parallel of Deism and Classicism" (135). Argues that Lovejoy tended "to confuse deism with rational Christianity," that "deism was less closely related to neo-classicism than Lovejoy suggested," that "a case can be made for the closer affinity or parallel of classicism and Christianity," and that "the sources of deism and neo-classicism were separate." In spite of his criticism of Lovejoy's conclusions in this instance, Stromberg asserts that with "Lovejoy's program and method there can surely be no real quarrel."

Stromberg continues to believe that they were not in some important respects.

434. Wigmore, John H. "Academic Freedom of Utterance."  $ \underline{\text{Nation}} $, 103 (1916), 538-40.

Argues that there is an analogy between a judge's protection from civil action as a result of his rulings and a professor's right to academic freedom. The protection accorded professors must, however, include the incompetent as well as the competent, the radical as well as the conservative. One can not make distinctions based on the quality of the professor or on the nature of the utterance. There are, nonetheless, some limitations to academic freedom. Scholars are protected only so long as they stay within their area of competence and the "utterance must have been made while doing some act of the strictly academic function." That is not to imply that professors give up their ordinary rights as citizens.
435. Wilson, Daniel J. "Arthur O. Lovejoy and the Moral of  $ \underline{\text{The Great Chain of Being.}} $"  $ \underline{\text{JHI}} $, 41 (1980), 249-65.

Argues that "The Great Chain of Being" is not merely the history of an idea, it is also the history of Lovejoy's ideas." Lovejoy's use of the history of ideas aided him in his effort "to create a rational and intelligible account of the world" by demonstrating that ideas do indeed exist and that man has used them to order his world. Lovejoy began his research in the complex of ideas he would trace in The Great Chain of Being (5) before 1902. By 1904, in the essay "The Dialectic of Bruno and Spinoza" (22), Lovejoy had outlined the framework of western thought he would later trace in greater detail. Though Lovejoy would greatly expand his research and strengthen his argument in the thirty years between the essay and the book, the structure of the argument and the moral of the history remained the same. The moral in both cases was the hopelessness of conceiving a total Absolute that included reality in its manifoldness and development. A wholly rational world was impossible, but a developmental world, a world of becoming, was not, and on that foundation Lovejoy built his philosophy.

436. ___. "Professionalization and Organized Discussion in the American Philosophical Association, 1900-1922." Journal of the History of Philosophy, 17 (1979), 53-69.

Traces the efforts of one group of philosophers within the American Philosophical Association to make the discipline more professional and more scientific in its methods. They attempted to achieve that goal in these years by organizing discussions at the annual meeting where, they hoped, the issue under discussion could be settled and the discipline could move on to other issues. Lovejoy was a leader among those pushing for a more scientific and professionalized discipline. Though he strongly defended his views in his 1916 presidential address (91), the movement for a more scientific philosophy achieved through organized discussion was dead by the early twenties. Those who supported the idea of a scientific philosophical discipline found other means to achieve their goals.

500. Gordon-Bournique, Gladys. "Arthur O. Lovejoy et l'histoire des idées." Ph.D. dissertation, The University of Paris, 1974. 217 pp.

Argues that knowledge of Lovejoy's work in France is slight and hopes to bring it to wider attention. Relying on extensive quotation, all translated into French, Gordon-Bournique describes Lovejoy's method, compares his essays with his methodological statements, examines Lovejoy's responses to criticisms of his approach, and attempts to assess the relationship of the history of ideas and of Lovejoy's philosophical views. temporalism was a key factor in his arguments against idealism. For the most part, Reitzner summarizes Lovejoy's arguments, with some reference to contemporary criticism. In the last chapter, Reitzner evaluates Lovejoy's argument against idealism and notes that "if one accepts the principle that one exception to a universal or total position or claim overthrows that position or claim ... This volume was put together by the critical realists in response to cooperative volumes published by the new realists (526) and the pragmatists (522). The contributors focused on epistemological questions and attempted to construct a theory of knowledge, or more accurately theories of knowledge, which avoided the problems inherent in monistic realism. Although the contributors are in general accord on the philosophical views they oppose, there is less agreement on the positive aspects of critical realism, even in the area of epistemology. The book does bring together the writings of these philosophers, including Lovejoy, which they wanted to be identified with critical realism.

Although the contributors are in general accord on the philosophical views they oppose, there is less agreement on the positive aspects of critical realism, even in the area of epistemology. The book does bring together the writings of these philosophers, including Lovejoy, which they wanted to be identified with critical realism.

Government during World War I. William James and Josiah Royce. Kuklick traces the development of pragmatism and attempts to elucidate its crucial doctrines. Beginning in the 1890s professionalism became an important factor influencing the development of philosophy and the character of the men attracted to the study of the discipline. Kuklick also traces the changes that came to Harvard after the "Golden Age" had passed, the impact of President A. This book provides a superb introduction into the intellectual milieu in which Lovejoy was trained and into the kind of philosophical and institutional pressures operating on all philosophers in the early twentieth century.

Offers a short historical sketch of the rise of philosophical realism in America in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century. This book is based, in Part, on his A History of American Philosophy (New York: Columbia University Press, 1946). Argues that the realistic movement "created enduring foundations for contemporary thinking," though since it was "foundational, realism is now less conspicuous." ### 532. Veysey, Laurence R.  $ \underline{\text{The Emergence of the American University}} $. Chicago: The University of Chicago Press, 1965. 505 pp.

Provides an account of the creation of the modern American university between 1865 and 1910 and of the academic reforms that worked to transform the liberal arts college into the modern research university. 533. Dunn, John. "The Identity of the History of Ideas."  $ \underline{\text{Philosophy}} $, 43 (1968), 85-104.

Attempts to define the characteristics of the history of ideas, by which he means a more general discipline than the methodology of Lovejoy. Argues that "the connection between an adequate philosophical account of the notions held by an individual in the past and an accurate historical account of these notions is an intimate one; that both historical specificity and philosophical delicacy are more likely to be attained if they are pursued together." Provides most of his evidence from the history of political thought.
534. Flenley, Ralph. "History and Ideas."  $ \underline{\text{Transactions of the Royal Society of Canada}} $, 40, Section 2 (May 1946), 43-55.

Traces the ways in which "historians have concerned themselves or should concern themselves with ideas and their development." Surveys various examples from the ancient Greeks to the early twentieth century. Lovejoy is not mentioned directly.
535. Holborn, Hajo. "The History of Ideas."  $ \underline{\text{AHR}} $, 73 (1968), 683-95.

Reviews the history of the history of ideas beginning with Voltaire. Argues that Wilhelm Dilthey was the "greatest historian of ideas [and] ... his influence in this field has been extraordinary." Believes that Dilthey's historical work derived from his philosophical interests. Sees social history as a necessary adjunct to intellectual history.
536. Krieger, Leonard. "The Autonomy of Intellectual History."  $ \underline{\text{JHI}} $, 34 (1973), 449-516.

Attempts to define the characteristics of contemporary intellectual history, such as Lovejoy's method in the history of ideas. Traces the development of the various forms of intellectual history in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Concludes by discussing the current approaches to intellectual history.

537. Lasch, Christopher. "The Cultural Cold War: A Short History of the Congress for Cultural Freedom." The Agony of the American Left. New York: Vintage Books, 1969, pp. 63-114.

Traces the history of the Congress for Cultural Freedom, organized in 1950. Argues that the affiliated American Committee for Cultural Freedom "represented a coalition of liberals and reactionaries who shared a conspiratorial view of communism and who agreed, moreover, that the communist conspiracy had spread through practically every level of American society." Lovejoy, to the extent that his declining health permitted, supported the activities of the American Committee for Cultural Freedom. This essay provides historical perspective on his activities.

See 313.
538. Mohr, James C. "Academic Turmoil and Public Opinion: The Ross Case at Stanford."  $ \underline{\text{Pacific Historical Review}} $, 39 (1970), 39-61.

Provides a discussion of the controversy over the dismissal of E.A. Ross at Stanford in 1901 during which Lovejoy resigned his position at the university in protest. Argues that Ross's manipulation of public opinion was crucial to the notoriety of the case.
539. Phelan, Gerald B. "Philosophy and the History of Ideas." Transactions of the Royal Society of Canada, 40, Section 2 (May 1946), 21-29.

Describes the relationship of philosophy and the history of ideas as a three-fold one depending on one's view of philosophy. The relation may be one of identity, one of creation ("philosophy makes ideas and their history"), or one of transcendence, ("philosophy is neither the cause nor the effect of the history of ideas but transcends it"). Though one can find examples of all three types of relation, Phelan concludes that "in its essence, philosophy transcends time and seeks eternal truth, though its effort to achieve it must suffer the vicissitudes of time and share in the development of human knowledge."
